To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the stability of IsicU, a bacterial protein highly conserved and involved in iron–sulfide cluster biosynthesis, is strongly affected by its zinc content, which is in turn determined by the sample history, and by the presence of other metal ions in the solution, and that the zinc content can be finely modulated by the presence of different side chains, all competent to coordinate zinc, and by local structural rearrangements.
IscU is marginally stable, that zinc binding stabilizes the IsdU fold, and that zinc can cause protein aggregation when added back posthumous.
IscU is marginally stable, that zinc is a strong stabilizing factor for IscU, and that the effect of the zinc depends on the sample history.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role played by metal coordination in the stability of IschU, a scaffold protein involved in the biogenesis of iron–sulfure clusters.
the role of zinc in protein stability and aggregation and how this role can be influenced by the sample history.
the role of metal ions in protein stability and how the metal coordination can affect protein folding and aggregation.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
IscU is an intrinsically disordered protein that can be stabilized by zinc and that the stability of Iscu is a function of the sample history.
zinc binding is a stabilizing factor in IscU, and that the protein is a marginally folded protein that can undergo cold denaturation.
zinc is a stabilizer of IscU but not a protector against cold denaturation, which is in agreement with the fact that IscU does not bind zinc in the cell.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
zinc binding to the IscU scaffold is a key event in the iron–sulphur cluster biogenesis and that the stability of Iscu is crucial to ensure its proper function.
the IscU scaffold is a very flexible protein that can undergo large rearrangements, which are stabilized by zinc and/or by the binding of a partner protein.
the stability of the IscU scaffold is determined by the delicate interplay of the intrinsic protein fold and the metal coordination.
The main takeaway from our work is that
zinc coordination is a key factor for the stability of IsdU, which is consistent in turn with the evolutionary pressure exerted by the environment on the protein.
the stability of a protein can be strongly dependent on sample history and that this can be a major issue in protein engineering.
IscU is an intrinsically marginally stable protein, and that zinc is a key player in the stabilization process.
